Comfort Peter emerged as the best graduating student of the Faculty of Arts at the University of Uyo in 2025. She speaks to TEMITOPE ADETUNJI about her journey to academic excellence, the challenges she overcame, the mentors who inspired her and her plans for the future. What was growing up like for you? I am an indigene of Akwa Ibom State, and growing up there was a beautiful experience. The state is known for its peaceful atmosphere and the warmth of its people. Akwa Ibom people are generally welcoming, disciplined and hardworking. I particularly enjoy our local delicacies, which I miss whenever I am away from home. Respect is an important value in our culture. I was raised to respect elders, and greetings are taken seriously in our community. My life has largely revolved around Akwa Ibom, from my nursery education to tertiary education, church, friendships and work. It is a place I hold very dear because it has played a significant role in shaping my values. Why did you choose to study English and Literary Studies at the University of Uyo? I have always had a strong liking for the English Language, and it dates back to my primary and secondary school days. I was fascinated by its creative, flexible and versatile nature, particularly its ability to accommodate different expressions and communicate ideas in various ways. I also developed a deep love for literature. In secondary school, I always looked forward to our literature classes because our teacher had an exceptional ability to analyse literary texts and make them captivating. I was fascinated by how literature mirrored reality and how virtually anything could become a subject of literary exploration. I can confidently say that I have never regretted my decision to study the course. Many people thought it was my second choice, but that was not the case. It was actually the course I wanted to study at the university. When did you gain admission into the University of Uyo? It was in 2019. It marked the beginning of a new chapter filled with excitement and expectations. I graduated in 2025. My academic journey was extended by several interruptions, including the COVID-19 lockdown, the eight-month ASUU strike and other factors that affected the academic calendar. Although the delay was not always easy, I remained focused on completing my programme. The experience taught me patience and the importance of staying committed even when circumstances do not go according to plan. How would you describe your experience studying English and Literary Studies? I would say it was bittersweet. I will not pretend it was easy. English and Literary Studies has a broad scope, and some literature courses required us to read more than 30 literary texts and other materials for a single course. We had to attend lectures, submit assignments, write tests and examinations, and make class presentations, sometimes at short notice. The Department of English at the University of Uyo is strict and academically demanding. Our lecturers upheld high standards and did not encourage laziness or a casual attitude towards academic work. You have to earn every mark, and examination malpractice or sorting was not an option. Succeeding required dedication, determination and intentionality, alongside God’s grace. Despite the challenges, I genuinely enjoyed the experience. I particularly enjoyed the literature courses and the different arguments and perspectives they introduced. I also appreciated the language aspect, which exposed me to the structure and workings of English. Overall, it was a demanding but rewarding experience. At what point did you realise that graduating with a first class was achievable? I began to see graduating with a first class as a realistic possibility in the first semester of my second year. My CGPA increased from 4.42 in the first semester of my first year to 4.45 in the second semester, and eventually reached 4.52 in the first semester of my second year. This steady improvement encouraged me because it showed that my efforts were yielding results and that achieving a first class was within my reach. I eventually graduated with a final CGPA of 4.61. He helped me understand that graduating with a first class, even in a demanding department like ours, was achievable. He was already a first class student, and seeing what he had achieved inspired me to aim higher. His encouragement helped me move from simply hoping for good results to working towards a clear academic goal. What personal habits helped you maintain such an impressive academic record? One habit that helped me was preparing for each semester before it officially began. I made enquiries about the courses we would be offering, familiarised myself with their course codes and titles, sourced relevant study materials and past questions, and began studying ahead of time. This gave me a head start because I was already somewhat familiar with the courses when lectures commenced. I also surrounded myself with people who shared similar academic goals, and we formed a study group. We often made time to come to school and study together. Attending lectures was also non-negotiable for me. I took notes diligently, recorded lectures when necessary and paid attention to areas lecturers emphasised. This helped me identify topics that required particular attention when preparing for tests and examinations. Having a reading routine and asking questions whenever I needed clarification were equally important. I also had a mentor I could turn to for academic guidance. Beyond what we were taught or given in class, I conducted independent research to broaden my understanding of the subjects. Finally, prayer was an important part of my journey. I often prayed and committed my plans and endeavours into God’s hands, and He indeed crowned my efforts. These habits, combined with intentionality, dedication, resilience and God’s grace, contributed significantly to my performance. Preparation, rather than last-minute pressure, was one of the most important factors in my academic journey. What was the most challenging period of your undergraduate years? My third year was the most challenging, particularly the first semester. This was when my CGPA dropped significantly from 4.63 to 4.55, and I found it difficult to process. I felt discouraged because I had worked hard to maintain my academic performance. We offered fewer courses than students in other levels, but they were considerably more demanding. In the first semester, we offered six courses with very broad content, while in the second semester, we offered eight. One of them was Foreign Policy Analysis, a course borrowed from the Department of History. It was particularly challenging because I struggled to relate to the subject, but I eventually excelled in it. That period taught me that sometimes, even after putting in the necessary effort, we may not get the results we desire. However, I refused to allow the setback to define my academic journey. I kept going, remained committed to my studies and reminded myself that one difficult period did not erase my previous efforts or determine what I could still achieve. Were there moments when you doubted your academic abilities? Yes, I did. Throughout my undergraduate journey, there were moments when I felt tired, mentally exhausted and uncertain about my ability to keep up with the demands of the programme. The workload could be overwhelming, especially considering the volume of reading, assignments and academic expectations that came with studying English and Literary Studies. However, I learnt not to allow those moments of exhaustion to define my abilities or determine the outcome of my journey. I reminded myself of the goal I had set, drew strength from my faith and the encouragement of people who believed in me, and kept pushing forward. Looking back, those moments taught me resilience, patience and the importance of believing in myself, even when the journey became difficult. How did you balance your academic responsibilities with personal life and other commitments? Balancing everything was challenging, especially as someone actively involved in church activities and who also had responsibilities at home. I had several commitments competing for my time, so I had to learn to prioritise. I understood that I could not give every activity the same level of attention at every moment. I made my academics a major priority and deliberately created time to study, even when it was inconvenient. I learnt to make good use of the time available rather than waiting for the perfect moment. Preparing ahead, maintaining a reading routine and being intentional about my daily activities helped me stay on track. I would not say I got the balance right every time, but I learnt to manage my responsibilities without losing sight of my goals. The experience taught me that balance is not always about doing everything at once; it is about making thoughtful choices and remaining responsible. What does being named the Best Graduating Student in the Faculty of Arts mean to you? It means a great deal to me. Being the Best Graduating Student in a faculty comprising eight departments is a great honour, and I feel deeply grateful. Beyond the award, the achievement has reinforced my belief that my goals are attainable and my dreams are valid. It has reminded me that it is possible to achieve great things regardless of where one comes from or the circumstances surrounding one’s beginnings. Were there particular lecturers, mentors or individuals who played significant roles in your academic journey? Yes, there were. Above all, I am grateful to God, whose grace, strength and guidance carried me throughout my academic journey. I was fortunate to have lecturers who nurtured my curiosity and deepened my desire to learn. I particularly appreciate Dr Imo Okon, Prof Ini Uko, Prof Friday Okon, Prof Garvey Ufot, Prof Ima Immanuel and Dr Bernard Dickson, among others. Dr Imo Okon, who was my project supervisor, played an important role by guiding me through my research with helpful feedback and unwavering support throughout the writing process. One person who played a particularly significant role was my academic mentor, Tommy Nteowo. I met him in my first year, and he made a remarkable difference in how I viewed myself and my academic potential. He also challenged a stereotype I had associated with having a male school father as a female student. Tommy showed me that such a relationship could be built on genuine mentorship, mutual respect, care and commitment to a student’s growth, without being reduced to romantic or intimate expectations. At a time when making a first class in our department seemed almost impossible because of its strict academic standards and demanding examinations, Tommy encouraged me to think differently. He constantly reminded me that I could achieve that and even more. He encouraged me to aim for the best and distinguish myself rather than settle for what seemed ordinary. Indeed, I achieved even more than I initially imagined by graduating with first-class honours and being named the Best Graduating Student in both my department and faculty. One mindset he instilled in me was to approach every course as an A course. Rather than limiting myself or doubting my abilities, I began each course with the expectation that I could excel. He explained literature and language courses I struggled with, guided me on answering examination questions and offered valuable advice on my seminars and project. I am immensely grateful for his patience, sacrifices and confidence in me. I often say, “God bless the day I met him,” because he helped shape my academic journey and taught me to believe that excellence was attainable. I also had other wonderful people who supported me throughout my academic journey. My parents did so much for me, and I am deeply grateful for their sacrifices, love and unwavering support. My family and little community were incredibly supportive, and I am especially grateful to my godmother, who invested so much in my education. I was equally fortunate to have amazing friends who made the journey lighter in their own ways. They include Patrick, Goodnews, Abas, Shola, Ezekiel, Esther and my school sister, Justine. Their kindness and presence meant a great deal to me, and I do not take any of it for granted. Looking back, I realise that my academic journey was not one I undertook alone. It was made easier and more meaningful by the people who believed in me, stood by me and contributed in one way or another to the person I have become. I remain deeply grateful to every one of them. What misconceptions do you think people have about studying English and Literary Studies? I think there are several misconceptions about studying English and Literary Studies. One is the assumption that it is simply about learning to speak and write good English, whereas the discipline goes much deeper, covering language, linguistics, literary criticism, creative writing and the relationship between language, society and human experiences. Another misconception is that it is an easy course because English is a language we use daily. People often overlook the extensive reading, research, critical thinking, interpretation and analysis involved. Some also assume that studying literature is merely about reading stories and novels for entertainment, without recognising its role in helping us understand society, culture, history, human behaviour and different aspects of life. Finally, there is the belief that graduates of the discipline can only become teachers or that the course has little relevance outside the classroom. In reality, the skills acquired are applicable to several fields, including journalism, publishing, broadcasting, public relations, communication and research. English and Literary Studies equips students with valuable skills that are relevant in virtually every professional field. What are you currently doing? I am currently undergoing the National Youth Service Corps programme, where I have the opportunity to gain practical experience and contribute my knowledge and skills through service. What are your plans for the future? My plans after NYSC are to take deliberate steps towards building a fulfilling career and advancing my education. I hope to secure opportunities that will allow me to grow professionally, gain practical experience and make meaningful contributions wherever I find myself. I also intend to pursue further studies because my passion for learning has not ended with my undergraduate degree. I want to remain connected to academia, whether through further studies, teaching or other opportunities that allow me to contribute to learning and knowledge. While I may not have every step mapped out yet, I am committed to making the most of the opportunities that come my way and continually working towards becoming a better version of myself. I believe growth is a continuous process, and I look forward to the next phase of my journey. Temitope Adetunji Temitope Adetunji is a journalist at Punch Newspapers who specialises in human-interest storytelling.
